clue.text: See 19
It briefly holds story in crazy ordeal

parts.note: nuts is slang for crazy
a hellish experience is an ordeal; hell can mean any torment

explanation.surface: A tale set inside some maddening trial, as if the narrator were going through hell.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'in a nutshell', meaning briefly: a story told in a nutshell is held there in short form.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic: to tell a story 'in a nutshell' is to put it briefly, so the shell is what holds it.

clue.text: Financial supporter recycled no art under pressure

indicators.note: in a down clue the reworked letters sit beneath the pressure symbol

parts.note: P is the standard physics symbol for pressure

indicators.note: recycled material is reused in a new form, so these letters are remade in a different order

explanation.surface: A backer of the arts pulls out, turning recycled junk into something other than art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recycled' rearranges NO ART into ATRON, and 'under' places it below P in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A patron is a sponsor or benefactor who funds an artist or institution, i.e. a financial backer.

clue.text: Old French painter coming up short

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means read from bottom to top, i.e. backwards
short means missing its final letter, so the painter's name loses its last one

parts.note: Edgar Degas, the French Impressionist painter of ballet dancers

explanation.surface: An elderly French artist whose career is falling short as he climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts DEGAS to DEGA, and 'coming up' turns that over to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple synonym: something old has lived or lasted a long time, i.e. is elderly.

clue.text: Eg, marriage and love in western capital

parts.note: marriage is one of the Christian sacraments, given here as an example
love is zero in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A wedding and romance out in the American West, perhaps in a state capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eg' marks marriage as an example of a sacrament. The city is the capital of California.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacramento is the state capital of California, in the western United States.

clue.text: Provides backing for tracks about partners holding hands

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the tracks word goes round the partners

parts.note: spoor is the track or trail left by an animal
in bridge, North and South are partners, each holding a hand of cards

explanation.surface: Couples walking hand in hand along trails, and someone funding them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding hands' looks like affection but is bridge: North and South are partners, each holding a hand. 'about' wraps the animal tracks round them.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponsor is to support financially, so 'provides backing for' is the verb in the same third-person form.

clue.text: Pseudonymous author and his state

definitions.meaning: Anatole ..., pen name of the French novelist Jacques Anatole Thibault
the author's pen name is also the name of his own country

explanation.surface: A writer hiding behind a pen name, and the condition he is in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like condition, but means nation: Anatole France took his country's name as his pen name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatole France wrote under a pseudonym, and the same word names the nation he came from.

clue.text: How one plays after first-half switch in this European city

indicators.note: the first half of the word is swapped round, its two letters exchanging places

parts.note: playing solo is playing alone, as one person

explanation.surface: A musician describing how they perform alone in a European city after swapping halves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after first-half switch' turns only the first two letters of SOLO, SO becoming OS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital city of Norway, in northern Europe.

clue.text: Rule again broken, resulting in complaint

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: Someone breaks a rule a second time, and a grievance follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complaint' looks like a grievance, but here it is a medical complaint, an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Neuralgia is nerve pain, and a complaint in the medical sense is an illness or ailment.

clue.text: Old prince's moveable feast, so-called

definitions.meaning: The Trojan prince of Greek legend who carried off Helen
Hemingway's memoir A Moveable Feast called the French capital by that name

explanation.surface: An ancient prince's feast, one that can be moved about, as it is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moveable feast' sounds like a church holiday such as Easter, but here it is Hemingway's title for the city in his memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trojan prince of the Iliad and the city Hemingway called a moveable feast share one name.

clue.text: Hardened about son being protected against loss

indicators.note: about means around, so the hardened word wraps the son

parts.note: inured means toughened or accustomed to hardship

explanation.surface: A tough parent wraps a son up safely against any misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts INURED around S.
explanation.definitionFit: Insured property is covered by a policy that pays out if it is lost or damaged.

clue.text: Encountered artist and Cuban American writer also, we hear

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
Anaïs Nin, the diarist born in France to Cuban parents and later American

indicators.note: we hear signals that a word is said aloud and spelt as another that sounds the same

parts.note: too means also

explanation.surface: Bumped into a painter and a Cuban American author as well, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns TOO into TO by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Phrasal verb synonym: to run into someone is to meet them by chance.

clue.text: Author that can hold a lot of beer

definitions.text: that can hold a lot of beer
definitions.meaning: a large earthenware beer mug, often holding a litre

explanation.surface: A writer with a large capacity for ale.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is Gertrude Stein, whose sayings run through this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude Stein is the writer, and the same word names a big German-style beer mug.

clue.text: About to drop off original Monets, number left inside

indicators.note: inside means the abbreviations are placed within the rearranged letters
original here means new and inventive, so the painter's name is rearranged into fresh form

explanation.surface: Original Monets are about to be dropped off, with a number left inside the crate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original' reads as genuine paintings but signals the anagram, giving SOMENT; 'About to drop off' is the definition, not a delivery.
explanation.definitionFit: Somnolent means drowsy, sleepy enough that one is close to nodding off.

clue.text: Thus covering match is absurdly divisive

indicators.note: covering means surrounding, so the Latin word goes round the shuffled letters

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus, used to mark a quotation as printed

indicators.note: absurdly means ridiculously, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A match covered in this way proves absurdly divisive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thus' is the Latin sic, used in quotations; 'absurdly' gives CHISMAT for 'covering' to enclose.
explanation.definitionFit: Schismatic describes something causing a split, as in a church schism, hence divisive.

clue.text: At that point, repeated consoling words

indicators.note: repeated means said twice over, so the word appears two times in a row

parts.note: there means at that place or point

explanation.surface: At some moment, the same comforting phrases are said over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer also echoes Gertrude Stein's line about Oakland, 'there is no there there'.
explanation.definitionFit: Said to soothe a crying child or upset friend, the doubled phrase is a stock expression of comfort.

clue.text: Ready for early retirement

parts.note: ready is slang for cash, so this is a cash payment given to someone who retires early

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective meaning prepared, but it is the noun 'the ready', British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous lump-sum payout made to an executive leaving a company, often on early retirement.

clue.text: Exhilarated and happy about Eliot's first verse

indicators.note: about means around, so the happy word wraps the other letters

parts.note: elated means very happy

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the poet's name is used

explanation.surface: A reader feels joy at T. S. Eliot's early poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eliot's first' gives E, and 'about' puts ELATED around E and V.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevated can mean in high spirits, lifted up emotionally, much like exhilarated.

clue.text: Drink consumed around 13, tipsily?

indicators.note: around means the eaten word goes round the other letters

parts.note: consumed means ate

indicators.note: tipsily means drunkenly, so the mug's letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: 13 across is the beer mug, also the theme author

explanation.surface: Someone downs a beer mug's worth, staggering a little afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 13 is used for its letters, not its sense: 'tipsily' gives NISET, which 'around' puts inside the eating word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is an aniseed-flavoured liqueur, a type of alcoholic drink.

clue.text: A resolution's not apparent — hence sigh?

parts.note: the word sight with no end letter becomes sigh, so this little word shows the phrase in action

explanation.surface: Nothing gets resolved, so somebody sighs in frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing question 'hence sigh?' is the joke: take the end off 'sight' and you are left with a sigh.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: when a problem or conflict seems never to be ending, no solution can be seen coming.

clue.text: End of line for some, including setter and solver in old school

indicators.note: including means holding within, so the school goes round the pair

parts.note: Eton College, the ancient English public school
the setter and the solver together are us

explanation.surface: A school leaver's journey's end, with us two once pupils at an old school.
explanation.walkthrough: EUSTON is a London railway terminus, where some train lines end. Eton is the famous English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Euston is a London mainline terminus, so trains on its lines finish their journey there.

clue.text: Girl having nibble from cake in a story

indicators.note: in means the bitten letter is placed inside the other words

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story, a fib

indicators.note: a nibble is a tiny bite, so only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A girl takes a bite of cake in a tale, like Carroll's heroine in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Wonderland, but 'a story' is A LIE, and 'nibble from' takes just C, which 'in' places inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A common female first name, so it stands for any girl.

clue.text: Female novelist in same state as 20, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means a word spoken aloud and spelt another way

parts.note: the station name sounds like Houston, a Texas city, and Austin is in Texas too

explanation.surface: A woman writer living in the same state as some other place, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 20, EUSTON, is said like Houston; Austin, the Texas capital, shares its state, and 'we hear' turns it into the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen, author of Pride and Prejudice, is a celebrated English woman writer of novels.

clue.text: Callas ruined a great operatic scene

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Maria Callas spoiled a great moment in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scene' looks like a stage scene, but here it is a setting: the Milan opera house.
explanation.definitionFit: La Scala in Milan is one of the world's most famous opera houses, a grand venue for opera.

clue.text: Top player thrashed when 19 15

indicators.note: with 19 the phrase begins there is no..., so the word is removed

parts.note: leathered is slang for beaten or thrashed
15 down supplies the word to be taken out

explanation.surface: The star performer was beaten when things got hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with the cross-references, the clue says 'thrashed when there is no THERE', echoing Stein's line: take THERE out of LEATHERED.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead is the principal performer in a play or film, the star of the show.

clue.text: Earnestly ask what's inside nest in tree

indicators.note: in means the middle letters are placed within the tree

parts.note: the beech is a common tree

indicators.note: the inside of a word is its letters without the first and last

explanation.surface: Pleading to know what is inside a bird's nest up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests eggs or chicks, but 'what's inside' means the word's middle letters; 'in' places them after the B of the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: To beseech is to beg or implore someone urgently and earnestly.

clue.text: Objection about what's repeated in Picasso's sculptural work

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the objection goes round the letter

parts.note: but is used to raise an objection, as in 'no buts'
the only letter appearing twice in that name is S

explanation.surface: A complaint about the repetitiveness of a Picasso sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts BUT around S, the letter doubled in Picasso.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a sculpture of a person's head, shoulders and chest.

clue.text: Conclusion of 13's tautology came up

definitions.meaning: Stein wrote 'Rose is a rose is a rose is a rose', a famous repetition ending with these words
past tense of rise, to get up or emerge

explanation.surface: The ending of an author's repetitive line was raised.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude Stein's line 'a rose is a rose is a rose' ends on the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of rise: something that came up has risen, like the sun or an issue.

clue.text: Officer and cop involved with 13, right?

indicators.note: involved means tangled up together, so the two sets of letters are mixed

parts.note: 13 across is the author and beer mug

explanation.surface: A policeman, a cop, gets entangled with a beer drinker, rightly so?
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is the beer mug, used only for its letters: 'involved with' mixes them with the cop's to give INSPECTO.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector is a police officer ranking above a sergeant.
